implementation_notes: Java's instrument is `mvn dependency:analyze`, which reports used-undeclared and declared-unused dependencies; the declaration half is exactly the boat-anchor half. The Java-specific traps are reflection (Spring's component scanning, Jackson, JPA) and the classloader, so a class that no code names can still be instantiated by the framework — and a class loaded by a `Class.forName` string is live regardless of what any import says. Unused-field and unused-private-method warnings are configured rather than default in most builds, which is why so many accumulate. An unused `Serializable` class or an unused `serialVersionUID` is the classic harmless-looking anchor.
idiom_name: unused Maven dependency, unused class, obsolete listener registration
code_sketch:
<!-- dependency declared but imported nowhere -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId><artifactId>legacy-reports</artifactId>
</dependency>
$ mvn dependency:analyze   -> "Unused declared" is the anchor list
pitfalls: `dependency:analyze` reports false positives for anything loaded reflectively; the fix is to configure exclusions, not to ignore the whole report.
A dependency pulled in only for tests still ships in some build layouts, so it must be moved to `test` scope or removed.
Service-loader `META-INF/services` files make a class live with no import anywhere in the codebase.
